notes.bp: A speech recognizer for a device with little compute should remain useful without the memory and delay of a large model.
notes.wh: Accuracy, model size, latency, and energy pull in different directions, especially when training data and target hardware are limited.
notes.naive: Shrink a large model after training or use a tiny architecture and accept that accuracy is unrelated to the resource budget.
notes.ap: Design a training framework that improves lightweight ASR while measuring the accuracy-resource tradeoff directly.
notes.mech: The paper proposes an effective training framework for lightweight automatic speech-recognition models.
notes.math: Efficiency is a constraint on the whole training-and-inference pipeline: the model must spend its limited capacity on speech distinctions that matter for the target device.
notes.ww: The paper reports lightweight ASR accuracy and resource results for the proposed framework.
notes.limits: Hardware, language, model family, data, latency measurement, and compression settings limit generalization; a benchmark model is not a deployment guarantee.
notes.title: An Effective Training Framework for Light-Weight Automatic Speech Recognition Models

notes.bp: People with congenital lip paralysis may produce acoustically similar speech using different articulatory movements, so sound alone can hide physical uniqueness.
notes.wh: The acoustic-to-articulatory mapping is many-to-one and compensatory; a stable sound does not imply a normal or shared production mechanism.
notes.naive: Classify the voice from acoustics alone or assume one acoustic pattern corresponds to one articulatory configuration.
notes.ap: Compare acoustic similarity with articulatory measurements in individuals with congenital lip paralysis to identify compensatory production mechanisms.
notes.mech: The paper studies acoustic similarities and articulatory uniqueness in speech production by individuals with congenital lip paralysis.
notes.math: Speech production is an inverse problem with compensation: the same acoustic target can arise from different physical routes, so articulatory evidence changes the interpretation of similarity.
notes.ww: The paper reports acoustic and articulatory findings for the affected speakers and comparison conditions.
notes.limits: Cohort, anatomy, language, tasks, imaging or motion measures, and acoustic metrics limit clinical generalization; similarity is not a diagnosis.
notes.title: Acoustic similarities, articulatory uniqueness: Speech production mechanisms in individuals with congenital lip paralysis

notes.bp: An ASR transcript should preserve laughter and speech-laugh events because they affect meaning, turn timing, and conversational analysis.
notes.wh: Ordinary ASR training treats non-lexical laughter as noise or deletion, while speech-laugh blends vocalization and words in ways that do not fit a simple token.
notes.naive: Remove laughter before recognition or fine-tune only on ordinary words and infer laughter from punctuation.
notes.ap: Fine-tune open-source ASR models with laughter and speech-laugh examples and evaluate how transcript enhancement changes these events.
notes.mech: The paper enhances open-source ASR transcripts through fine-tuning with laughter and speech-laugh.
notes.math: The transcript target expands from words to interactional vocal events; the model must preserve an event boundary and its overlap with lexical speech.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved handling of laughter and speech-laugh in the tested ASR transcripts.
notes.limits: Annotation scheme, language, laughter types, model, data mixture, and transcript use case bound the result; event recognition is not a full emotion or intent analysis.
notes.title: Enhancing Transcripts of Open-Source Automatic Speech Recognition Models Through Fine-Tuning with Laughter and Speech-Laugh

notes.bp: A speech classifier can be compromised by a hidden trigger in compressed audio, causing a targeted wrong label while ordinary tests still look normal.
notes.wh: Compression changes the waveform and may hide or reveal trigger patterns; an attacker wants the backdoor to survive the front-end while avoiding detection.
notes.naive: Test clean accuracy only or assume compression destroys every malicious perturbation.
notes.ap: Demonstrate and analyze a backdoor attack on deep speech classification through audio compression, including its clean-task and triggered behavior.
notes.mech: CBA studies a backdoor attack on deep speech classification via audio compression.
notes.math: The front-end becomes part of the attack surface: a transformation assumed to be harmless can carry a trigger that changes the classifier's decision.
notes.ww: The paper reports attack success and clean-task behavior for the tested compression-based backdoor.
notes.limits: Model, compression, trigger, target class, defenses, and threat model bound the claim; one attack does not establish universal vulnerability.
notes.title: CBA: Backdoor Attack on Deep Speech Classification via Audio Compression

notes.bp: A multilingual ASR model should adapt efficiently to a language without overwriting what it knows about other languages.
notes.wh: Languages compete for shared parameters and have uneven data; full fine-tuning is costly and can cause interference or forgetting.
notes.naive: Fine-tune the entire model for each language or use one shared update for every language.
notes.ap: Use language-specific LoRA experts so a shared base retains common speech structure while small expert updates handle language-specific differences.
notes.mech: The paper proposes efficient multilingual ASR fine-tuning via LoRA language experts.
notes.math: Parameter-efficient adaptation allocates change selectively: shared parameters carry reusable acoustics while experts absorb language-specific pronunciation and decoding behavior.
notes.ww: The paper reports multilingual ASR accuracy and efficiency results for LoRA language experts.
notes.limits: Languages, data balance, rank, routing, base model, and evaluation domains bound the claim; parameter efficiency does not guarantee fairness across languages.
notes.title: Efficient Multilingual ASR Finetuning via LoRA Language Experts

notes.bp: A front-end speech algorithm may improve intelligibility or remove noise but leave artifacts that make the final speech sound unpleasant; a refiner should improve perceived quality without undoing the front-end benefit.
notes.wh: Perceptual quality is hard to predict from signal metrics, and refinement can hallucinate detail or alter speech content.
notes.naive: Optimize one waveform metric or apply a generic denoiser after every front-end.
notes.ap: Use SpeechRefiner to learn perceptual quality refinement for outputs from varied front-end algorithms and evaluate quality and faithfulness.
notes.mech: SpeechRefiner targets perceptual quality refinement for front-end speech algorithms.
notes.math: Refinement is a second-stage correction problem: the input already contains a useful transformation, so the model must remove artifacts while preserving the first stage's content and gains.
notes.ww: The paper reports perceptual and signal-quality improvements for refined front-end outputs.
notes.limits: Front-end types, distortion, training targets, listeners, metrics, and content preservation bound the result; quality improvement is not guaranteed for unseen algorithms.
notes.title: SpeechRefiner: Towards Perceptual Quality Refinement for Front-End Algorithms

notes.bp: Autoregressive speech synthesis can sound good but take too long because it generates one token after another; users need faster inference without obvious quality loss.
notes.wh: Speculative decoding needs a fast proposal and an accurate verifier, and speech tokens have temporal dependencies that make incorrect guesses audible.
notes.naive: Generate fewer tokens by skipping steps or use a smaller model and accept a quality drop.
notes.ap: Use a fast speculative speech model to propose multiple tokens, then verify them with the target model and keep only accepted sequences.
notes.mech: The paper accelerates autoregressive speech-synthesis inference with speech speculative decoding.
notes.math: Speed comes from parallel verification rather than changing the target distribution blindly: accepted blocks preserve the large model's decisions while reducing serial work.
notes.ww: The paper reports inference-speed gains and quality behavior for speculative speech decoding.
notes.limits: Tokenization, proposal model, acceptance rate, hardware, speaker/style, and latency measurement bound the result; speedups vary with the workload.
notes.title: Accelerating Autoregressive Speech Synthesis Inference With Speech Speculative Decoding

notes.bp: A bilingual listener may learn that a spoken word refers to one visible object, but a model trained across languages can develop a different bias about whether labels are shared or exclusive.
notes.wh: Visual grounding combines language, vision, and bilingual experience; correlations in a dataset can make a model prefer one interpretation without representing the underlying referent.
notes.naive: Measure only retrieval accuracy or assume a bilingual model follows human word-learning biases automatically.
notes.ap: Test mutual-exclusivity behavior in bilingual visually grounded speech models using controlled novel-object and label situations.
notes.mech: The paper studies mutual exclusivity bias in bilingual visually grounded speech models.
notes.math: The task probes how a model allocates a new label when familiar labels already exist; its choice reveals an interaction between language-specific priors and visual evidence.
notes.ww: The paper reports mutual-exclusivity behavior and cross-language differences for the tested bilingual grounded models.
notes.limits: Languages, training data, object stimuli, model architecture, prompt/task design, and bias measure bound the claim; model behavior is not a direct account of child learning.
notes.title: The mutual exclusivity bias of bilingual visually grounded speech models
